Covariance matrices for an analytic multiscale fit

Source: R/profile_glm_uncertainty.R
vcov.multiScaleR.Rd

Return the covariance matrix of the estimated parameters from a multiScale_optim() fit made with an analytic backend. The joint matrix covers the kernel parameters and the regression coefficients together, and it is what predict.multiScaleR() uses for joint uncertainty. The conditional matrix covers the coefficients with the kernel parameters held at their estimates. multiScaleR-prediction explains when each kind of uncertainty applies.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR'
vcov(object, type = c("joint", "conditional"), ...)

Arguments

object

A multiScaleR fit from backend = "profile_glm" or backend = "joint_nb2". A backend = "joint_mixed" fit returns only native conditional covariance; its scale standard errors are in object$scale_est. Other backends raise an error. Use vcov(object$opt_mod) for their coefficient covariance conditional on the selected scales.

type

"joint" (the default) or "conditional".

  • "joint" returns the observed-information covariance of the log kernel parameters, the regression coefficients, and the log dispersion when the family has one.

  • "conditional" returns the coefficient covariance with the kernel parameters held fixed and the dispersion estimated. At the exact Poisson boundary of a "joint_nb2" fit it also holds the dispersion at that boundary, and joint covariance is unavailable there.

...

Passed to native vcov() for "joint_mixed". Otherwise unused.

Value

A numeric covariance matrix with named rows and columns, as described in Details. For "joint_mixed" with type = "conditional", the native glmmTMB covariance list, one matrix per model component, conditional on the selected scales.

Read the joint matrix

Rows and columns are named by parameter:

  • log_scale:<covariate>: log(sigma / u), the natural log of that covariate's sigma after dividing it by the internal distance unit u = object$kernel_inputs$unit_conv. Dividing by u shifts the log by a constant, so the variance equals the variance of log(sigma) in map units.

  • log_shape:<covariate>: the log shape parameter, for kernel = "expow".

  • beta:<term>: a regression coefficient on the link scale, named after its model-matrix column, for example beta:(Intercept). A standardized kernel-weighted covariate's coefficient describes one standard deviation of that covariate.

  • A final dispersion row when the family has one: log_theta for a negative binomial model and log_residual_sd for a Gaussian model.

The square root of a diagonal element is a standard error on that parameter's scale. For sigma, a 95% Wald interval in map units is sigma x exp(-1.96 x SE) to sigma x exp(1.96 x SE), where SE is the standard error of log_scale. These are the limits that summary(object) reports, and object$scale_est$SE is sigma x SE. Off-diagonal elements show how the estimates trade off, and stats::cov2cor() turns them into correlations.

Joint covariance is unavailable for fits at a parameter bound or when the identifiability checks fail. In that case type = "joint" raises an error that lists object$uncertainty$reasons, rather than reporting a misleading Wald result. The conditional matrix remains available.

One exception applies to both backends. When kernel parameters at a search bound are the only failed check, the joint matrix holds those parameters fixed at their bounds. Their rows and columns are zero, and the other rows and columns come from the observed information with the bounded parameters removed. That reduced information must pass the remaining checks. The matrix then carries a conditional_on attribute that names the bounded parameters, as does object$uncertainty$joint_conditional_on. A zero there means the parameter was held fixed, not that it is known exactly, and its standard error is missing in object$scale_est. The other standard errors are no wider than they would be if the bounded scale were free to vary, so treat them as conditional on that scale. A dispersion bound, every kernel parameter at a bound, or any other failed check still withholds joint covariance.

Read the conditional matrix

The conditional matrix holds only the beta: rows. It answers how uncertain the coefficients are if the scales of effect are exactly their estimates, which is also what vcov(object$opt_mod) and summary(object$opt_mod) describe.

See also

predict.multiScaleR() for predictions that use these matrices, multiScaleR-prediction, multiScale_optim(), and vignette("v09-estimates-and-intervals", package = "multiScaleR").

Examples

## Running example: counts at 100 survey points, two landscape layers
data("landscape_counts")
data("surv_pts")
pts <- terra::vect(surv_pts)
land <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                                package = "multiScaleR"))[[c("land1", "land2")]]
inputs <- kernel_prep(pts, land, max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian",
                      bin = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
dat <- data.frame(landscape_counts, inputs$kernel_dat)
start <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = dat)
fit <- multiScale_optim(start, inputs, backend = "profile_glm",
                        n_cores = 1, verbose = FALSE)

## Joint covariance of the two log scales and four coefficients
V <- vcov(fit)
round(V, 4)
#>                  log_scale:land1 log_scale:land2 beta:(Intercept) beta:site
#> log_scale:land1           0.0193          0.0011          -0.0002    0.0002
#> log_scale:land2           0.0011          0.0090          -0.0005   -0.0014
#> beta:(Intercept)         -0.0002         -0.0005           0.0083   -0.0016
#> beta:site                 0.0002         -0.0014          -0.0016    0.0070
#> beta:land1               -0.0009         -0.0020           0.0030   -0.0015
#> beta:land2                0.0014          0.0020          -0.0034    0.0001
#>                  beta:land1 beta:land2
#> log_scale:land1     -0.0009     0.0014
#> log_scale:land2     -0.0020     0.0020
#> beta:(Intercept)     0.0030    -0.0034
#> beta:site           -0.0015     0.0001
#> beta:land1           0.0068    -0.0008
#> beta:land2          -0.0008     0.0058

## 95% Wald limits for sigma, in meters, from the log-scale standard errors.
## They match the limits in summary(fit).
se_log <- sqrt(diag(V))[c("log_scale:land1", "log_scale:land2")]
sigma <- stats::setNames(fit$scale_est$Mean, rownames(fit$scale_est))
round(cbind(sigma, lower = sigma * exp(-qnorm(0.975) * se_log),
            upper = sigma * exp(qnorm(0.975) * se_log)))
#>       sigma lower upper
#> land1   238   182   313
#> land2   500   415   602

## Correlations show how the scale and coefficient estimates trade off
round(cov2cor(V), 2)
#>                  log_scale:land1 log_scale:land2 beta:(Intercept) beta:site
#> log_scale:land1             1.00            0.08            -0.02      0.02
#> log_scale:land2             0.08            1.00            -0.06     -0.17
#> beta:(Intercept)           -0.02           -0.06             1.00     -0.20
#> beta:site                   0.02           -0.17            -0.20      1.00
#> beta:land1                 -0.08           -0.26             0.40     -0.21
#> beta:land2                  0.13            0.28            -0.49      0.02
#>                  beta:land1 beta:land2
#> log_scale:land1       -0.08       0.13
#> log_scale:land2       -0.26       0.28
#> beta:(Intercept)       0.40      -0.49
#> beta:site             -0.21       0.02
#> beta:land1             1.00      -0.12
#> beta:land2            -0.12       1.00

## Coefficient standard errors with and without scale uncertainty
round(cbind(joint = sqrt(diag(V))[-(1:2)],
            conditional = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, type = "conditional")))), 3)
#>                  joint conditional
#> beta:(Intercept) 0.091       0.091
#> beta:site        0.084       0.082
#> beta:land1       0.082       0.079
#> beta:land2       0.076       0.072
